steps.title: Key Context
steps.body: The Historic Environment is a compulsory part of the Elizabethan England GCSE paper. Each year, the exam board specifies a particular Elizabethan site that students must study. The site changes every year, so you need to check which site is specified for your exam year. The Historic Environment question tests your ability to connect a physical place to the broader themes of Elizabethan history - understanding not just what a building looked like, but why it was built, what it tells us about Elizabethan society, and how it connects to the wider events of the period.

steps.title: Prodigy Houses
steps.body: The Elizabethan era saw the construction of enormous, lavishly decorated houses by wealthy courtiers. These were called "prodigy houses" because of their extraordinary size and magnificence. They were built partly as family homes, but also as venues to entertain the Queen during her annual "progresses" (royal tours around the country). The ability to host the Queen was a tremendous status symbol and a way for courtiers to demonstrate their loyalty and wealth.

steps.title: Key Principle
steps.body: Elizabethan buildings were never just functional - they were statements. A great house declared its owner's wealth and status. A church reflected the Religious Settlement. A castle demonstrated the government's commitment to defence. A House of Correction proclaimed the authorities' determination to control vagrancy. When writing about any site, always ask: What message was this building designed to send?

steps.title: Theme 1: Religion
steps.body: How does the site reflect the Religious Settlement of 1559? Church buildings show the shift from Catholic to Protestant worship: the removal of rood screens, statues, and wall paintings; the introduction of communion tables instead of altars; the use of English in services; the placement of the pulpit as the focal point (emphasising preaching). A site like a parish church or cathedral can demonstrate both the changes and the continuities in Elizabethan religious life.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: What are the three most important questions to ask about any Elizabethan building? (3 marks) | Explain how a great house like Hardwick Hall reflects the wealth of Elizabethan courtiers. (4 marks) | How does the design of an Elizabethan parish church reflect the Religious Settlement of 1559? (4 marks)

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always connect the specific site to the wider historical context - this is the most important thing Use the PEEL structure for each paragraph: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link Include specific named details about the site (dates, features, patrons) Check which site is specified for your exam year - it changes annually Don't just describe the building - explain its significance Always link back to the question's theme (wealth, religion, defence, culture, etc.) For "how far" questions, discuss evidence that supports AND challenges the statement Remember SPaG marks - write in clear paragraphs with correct spelling and punctuation Practise writing timed answers (approximately 20 minutes for 16+4 marks) Visit the site if possible, or use virtual tours and detailed photographs to build visual
